utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Jasna Denona.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, in November of 2000, did you have occasion to give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and did you sign that statement as accurate, and did you have occasion two days ago to review that statement and verify that it was in fact accurate?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer the statement of the witness into evidence pursuant to Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a statement which has been subject to the 92 bis procedure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. We had applied for 92 bis, but we have not done the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And so I have it right, the procedure under 92 bis had been granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The order, rather, had been granted, but no procedure had been followed. Very well. We'll consider that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions, but I'll read just a very brief summary of the statement. The witness lived her entire life in Bruska, which is east of Skabrnja and can be found on page 30 of the atlas. She was 15 years old at the time of the events in question. Bruska was a predominantly Croatian village with a view Serb houses, and was surrounded by predominantly Serb villages. She does not recall any problems between Croats and Serbs in her village before the events in question. On 21 December, 1991, in the evening there was a knock at the door of the house of the witness by men announcing themselves as the Krajina militia. The witness and her mother and two other women in the house fled out the back of the house. The men started shooting at the women, and the witness was shot in the hip and in the arm. Several hours later, the witness went to a neighbour's house and saw four men from her village who had been killed; Petar, Roko and Dusko Marinovic, and Sveto Draca. The witness later that evening had learned of others who had been killed in her village; Dragan and Ika Marinovic, and Krste Draca, Stana and Masa Marinovic. Aside from Sveto Draca who was a Serb JNA reserve, all of those who were killed that night were Croatian civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we should have an exhibit number for the 89(F) statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 575, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the registrar could give the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about the 92 bis (D) package of B-1345? Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miss Denona, you are testifying about events that took place at the end of 1991 when several citizens of Bruska, both Croats and Serbs, were killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. One gentleman was a Serb, the others were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the day those men were killed they were doing their normal housework, looking after cutting the meat?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Not the meat. They were doing the normal, regular chores.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then there was this armed attack when nine or ten persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One of those attacked survived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the police arrived immediately, as well as representatives of the judiciary, immediately after those events?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. They came 22 hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they came on the spot 22 hours after the event?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the first to arrive on site immediately transported the survivor to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't quite sure what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't transport anyone to hospital then except me, when the police from Benkovac arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they transported you to hospital.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And according to information collected by my associates, this one person was transported to the Knin hospital where he was treated and recovered, and after that he went to live in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That gentleman went on his own to the first neighbouring houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that gentleman Ante Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He went to the neighbouring Serbian village of Kalanje, and from there to hospital?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a Serb was killed on that occasion too, wasn't he? Sveto Draca. This is stated on the second page, paragraph 3, of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, Sveto Marinovic, among the other Croats, was also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this person who went to the Serbian village of Kalanje was Ante Marinovic, and he was a Croat and he was taken to the Knin hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You describe some moving scenes on page 3, in the last paragraph, when two neighbours, one a Serb and the other a Croat, cry over the bodies of their dead sons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll explain it in a moment for you. Around midnight, you say in your statement on page 3, the father arrived crying and said that he had found his wife and son Dragan killed in front of the house. Soon after that, Dejan Draca arrived, the father of Sveto Draca, and saw that Sveto had been killed too. So both Dragan Marinovic's father and Sveto Draca's father - Dragan is a Croat, Sveto a Serb - both of them had sons killed, they met there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is where they met, and they told us that they had been killed and it was quite natural for them to be distressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it clear then from what happened that there was a killed Serb and a Croat there, that this was done by -- I don't know what term to use -- a madman who didn't do it on an ethnic basis but somebody who was obviously disturbed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That is not the impression I have. It was also possible that the Serb man happened to be there by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you were immediately transported to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Not immediately. Twenty-two hours after I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "The ambulance took me to the health centre in Benkovac, and after that to the hospital in Knin. That night, they operated on my hip and arm. I spent about a week in the hospital. After that, I was discharged. With me in hospital was Ante Marinovic, and the Serb doctors treated us well and professionally. They told me to come later for further treatment. On the 10th of January, 1992, I went to hospital again. As there were no vacant beds, they couldn't admit me immediately, but I stayed with my former teacher until the 15th of March when I was admitted into hospital because of my arm." Then on the 17th, you were released from hospital and you returned home to Bruska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was transported to the hospital in Knin. The event we're talking about occurred on the 21st of December. I reached the hospital, however, on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's the next day.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the police also came there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, before the ambulance took me to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you spent the night in that house, "and the next day my mother and I returned to our home, and the ambulance arrived from Benkovac just before nightfall. With them was a woman who said she was from the police, and she asked what had happened."

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any event, the police did come. That was the police of Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that connection the police and judicial bodies instituted proceedings, an investigation to establish who was the perpetrator of this crime?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was established by the investigators that only one person had opened fire. That is why my assumption is that it must have been a deranged person. Do you know anything at all about the evidence pointing to a deranged person from another village who was a Serb, but the evidence seemed to point to him?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. At that point in time, there were several persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see those persons shooting, when you say there were several of them.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but through -- while I was talking to them through the closed door, and by the sounds, I concluded that there were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was absolutely no motive for any Serb soldier to have done any such thing, because a group of Croats and two Serbs were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: One Serb was killed, and I can't talk about the motives. I don't know what the motives were for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, and I assume this was an event that had a very bad impact on the local population, both Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, but only one Serb family was affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that political representatives and representatives of the military of the Serbs in Krajina publicly condemned that crime? There was an atmosphere of general condemnation of what had happened among officials and the population, both Serbs and Croats. The majority population there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, there was no grounds for me to come to such a conclusion, nor did I feel that people were disturbed by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did this crime is not known by the investigators nor the neighbours. Do you know anything about who were the perpetrators? As there was an investigation, my associates did not manage to discover the outcome of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They couldn't come to any results when probably there was no real investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there are people from Benkovac who would like to come and testify here because they care very much about removing from themselves and others the blame for such a crime?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 2, you say that someone knocked on the door and the voice seemed familiar, and you first thought that it was a joke.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That's right. That is what I thought, because I was a child and naive, and I never expected anything so awful to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The voice sounded familiar. On that basis, could you have any idea who it was knocking at the door?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that the killer was a local person from the village?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Somebody was saying something. It is not clear that he was a local, that he had necessarily to be from the village of Bruska. The inhabitants of the surrounding villages knew us as neighbours, neighbours who were Serbs, and they did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you were going say.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I was saying that the local inhabitants of surrounding villages knew the distribution of the houses and knew who lived where in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you heard that one voice of the person knocking on the door and he sounded familiar, could that point to the conclusion that the killer was alone?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, it can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say on page 2, paragraph 2, that the Serbs in Nadin and Skabrnja killed people in villages. Do you know at all what was happening in Nadin and Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, not too much. I was a child at the time, so I wasn't really interested in politics, nor did I pay any attention to such things or follow them with interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fighting that was going on in that area?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: There was fighting, and I do know that civilians were killed, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I fully appreciate the fact that you were very young at the time. Had you heard of Marko Miljanic who was commander of an independent battalion of Skabrnja and surrounding villages of Galovac, Gornica, Zemunik, and Nadin?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, even though you don't know the name, that units, these units that were in those localities numbered about 800 men under arms?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a conflict there between those units and the JNA, which was passing through from the immediate vicinities in Donja Zemunik? I assume there was a base there, there was a military JNA airport there in those days.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that because I didn't keep track of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all to the effect that before the actual fighting, on the 18th of November, 1991, members of this battalion captured more than 50 JNA soldiers and three officers?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. That is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you learn later, perhaps, that the commander of the Zadar sector, Josip Tulicic [phoen], gave instructions to the defence commander in Skabrnja, Marko Miljanic, that an attack be organised in the village on the JNA wherever they may appear, and that the fighting went on for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This event that you describe, what date was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The 21st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these battles were on the 18th of November. Do you remember that even though you were a child?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I remember the date, but battles ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember the battles?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in Skabrnja there were trenches dug out?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I didn't see them, so -- I know that a crime happened over there, but I don't know anything about the trenches or what you're aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aiming at anything. I'm -- you, in your statement, say that in villages some civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. This was on all TV stations, and one could see the victims who had been killed. So this is something that I didn't have to go and see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the fighting, in addition to members of the National Guards Corps, even civilians took part, including elderly people?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know anything at all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a report from the interview with the witness Marko Miljanic. I assume it was in Zadar. It wasn't to any particular JNA bodies, and it says: "From my battalion, out of the mobilised soldiers, 15 soldiers were killed and a certain number of elderly people who formally were not mobilised but who had weapons and some of them joined in at the right moment to defend the village," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know why that statement needed to be truthful nor why it could have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was given by Marko Miljanic, who was the commander of those units there on the spot in that place, as it says here. The municipal public prosecutor in Zadar, that means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had this several times already. There's absolutely no point asking a witness about what another witness says or the circumstances in which that other witness made a statement. All the witness can do is comment on the question which you ask, as she has done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Mr. May, but what I'm talking about are the circumstances, precisely because the witness has talked about the fact that people were killed in the villages, and from this statement we can see quite clearly that it wasn't given to the institutions of Krajina, it was given to none other than the Croatian authorities. And we can see that there was fighting there, how the fighting was conducted, and this is a document which I was given here, 0202773 is the page number, the ERN number, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point is that the witness cannot help you on these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the witness does not know that civilians took part in the fighting, including some elderly people as well, and this commander talks about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, regardless of the fact that you were very young at the time, did you have any idea at all about the fact that those forces used heavy weapons, mortars, and so on and so forth, and that it was a large unit in the area? You don't know any of these names, the names of the people who commanded those units at the time?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: On what side do you mean commanded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the National Guards Corps side and those units. You don't know any of the names?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know where Mate Drazen's house was?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before this fighting took place, the Zemunik airport was shelled, the military airport where the soldiers of the JNA were deployed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know, and as I said, I wasn't interested in things like that, nor did I follow events and attacks or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that it was precisely the soldiers of the JNA, when they were passing through the Croatian village of Gornji Zemunik, which joins up with Skabrnja - and we have this from different statements Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. presented here - didn't use any weapons? They didn't shoot at anyone, they just passed by, and it was only when they reached Skabrnja that they came across this unit and when they clashed with the unit.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know that either, so I can't say anything about it, because I wasn't there. I didn't pass that way at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were just passing by and then a conflict broke out, and a transport JNA vehicle was destroyed and that was in the frameworks of the then-large scale attacks on the JNA throughout Croatia at the time. Do you remember any of that or do you know about anything of that -- like that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. Had I been there, I probably would have known, or had I followed things like that, but like this I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the JNA soldiers who were killed and the officers who were killed during those conflicts at the time?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, to go back to the incident which you describe, later on was there an additional investigation undertaken of any kind with the judiciary of Zadar or with the Zadar police, or any of the authorities, and were they able to establish how the incident that you described came about, what had actually happened and who the possible perpetrator of the killing was?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The event happened, as I said, at the end of 1991, and the Zadar police force could have come into the area just in 1995 to investigate, so that they weren't able to conduct an investigation at the time, on the spot, to see what had actually happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, many things here are trying -- people are trying to reconstruct many things post festum, later on, but was an investigation ever conducted, because a number of people were, after all, killed in the incident. There were a number of casualties, people had lost their lives. So without doubt, it wasn't any -- due to any war operations but a classical crime had in fact been committed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. A great crime, that's right. A great crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a crime that has nothing to do with any military operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know whether it had anything to do with military operations or patients or mentally deranged patients or whatever I can call them. All I can say is what happened and what -- I described what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that the casualties were of mixed ethnicity, I think the logical conclusion was that it wasn't a killing that took place on a national ethnic basis but the way that I presented it as being a possibility. Do you allow for that possibility, that that might have been the way it happened?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: But as I said, there was only one Serb who was actually killed, and all the rest were Croats. And they came to a Croatian hamlet and not to a Serbian hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Denona, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, I should just like to ask you a few questions with respect to this specific event that you describe in the last paragraph of the second page of your statement. The English version is also on page 2. And you talk about the 21st of December, 1991, and you say that you went to the door when you heard somebody knocking.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To see who it was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say: "I asked, Who's there? and heard a male voice say the Krajina militia or police"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that, "the voice sounded familiar and I thought somebody was joking." That's what you say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't actually see who opened the door, and you don't know whether it was actually the militia or the police or not.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether it was the police, but the door was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you explained that, but you don't know who was on the other side of the door, and you don't know who the man at the door was who talked to Dragan, do you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And let me just ask you this: You said that only one Serb was killed and that the other casualties were Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that village, as you say in the third paragraph, there were only two houses inhabited by Serbs, the Draca family and another family. So there were no other families in that village.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Draca and Dobre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many families in all; just those two families?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: You mean how many family members in those two families?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 20, 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, you were asked some questions about Sveto Draca. Was he mobilised into the JNA reserves?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he mobilised willingly?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Not willingly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing at Roko Marinovic's house the night he was killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Nothing. They were just -- they just had a friendly meeting. They played some cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was -- was he there with his children?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You indicated that you thought that there was more than one person at the door when there was a knock. Can you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I can. The voice who answered me when I asked who was at the door was to my left. Judging by the sound of it, I came to the conclusion that he was on the left, whereas through the glass partition of the door I could see the outline, the silhouette, of another man. So I would say that the third person who shot a burst of gunfire was perhaps one or two metres away from the entrance door when they fired. So that I would say, in my assessment, there were more than two of them in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you ran out of the house and you were running in the yard, do you recall hearing somebody say something?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. A male voice said, "They're getting away from us. They're running away." And that's when they started shooting after us, and that's when I myself was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, there should be a correction made. 575 is the transcript and exhibits for B-1345, and that is under seal except for tab 1A which is a public redacted version of the transcript. And the statement for Witness Denona pursuant to Rule 89(F) is 576.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have one procedural matter we could do while the witnesses are changing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We have a 92 bis, full 92 bis statement to offer into evidence. It's of Witness C-1154 and it's full without cross-examination, and we would just like to tender the statement and the exhibits into evidence. There are protective measures, so I'm referring to the person by pseudonym and it needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 577, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is called, I'm afraid I find myself in the same position as Mr. Whiting, my learned colleague, in respect that Witness B-1780, who is coming, had actually been granted permission to give his evidence by way of bis, but with the Chamber's permission, I would kindly submit that he may have his statement submitted through Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that. While we're waiting, we'll ask the registrar to give the exhibit number for the new package.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 578 for the exhibit package.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: In order to save some time, Your Honours, may I request at this stage that the various exhibits to be tendered with this witness be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, may I kindly show the witness a pseudonym sheet, which you'll find at tab number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's wait until the blinds are up. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, could I kindly show the witness his pseudonym sheet, which you'll find in tab number 2 of your exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the pseudonym sheet where you're named as Witness B-1780, and can you confirm that that is your name, and the other matters listed there have been listed and signed by you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you give a statement before the Office of the Prosecution on 25th September 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: This can be found at tab 2 of Your Honours' bundle. Can the witness kindly be shown a copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could look at the last page of that statement, can you please confirm that that is your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And, Witness, for the purpose of certainty, you'll see by your signature a typed date of 25 September 1966. Can you please confirm for the Court that the year should, in fact, be 1996 rather than 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And on your arrival in The Hague, did you make a few variations to that statement, which is attached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, I'd just like to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: At the time of the incidents mentioned in this summary, the witness was living in Zvornik with his family. Branko Grujic, nicknamed Brano, was chairman of the SDS in Zvornik. The winter before the war, three or four unknown persons started to work in a shed near Grujic's bakery, which was near the woods. The witness saw these people practising their shooting in a nearby quarry. When the witness was later detained at Ekonomija farm, he recognised these people as being among Arkan's men. On the 12th of May, 1992, Niska, who was one of Arkan's men, took the witness to Ekonomija farm for questioning. The witness was taken to a building full of beaten-up men. All the men were naked. One man was dead, and the others were either moaning or crying. There were about between 18 to 20 men in the room, which was about 30 square metres in size. The witness recognised a number of the men. A man named Jasikovac, who had a Serbian accent, after speaking to Niski, brought in sticks which used to form part of a fence. The witness was beaten with these sticks until he became unconscious. The witness was then revived with water, dragged out of the building where he was about four feet away from one of his neighbours, Mr. Softic, whom he saw being beaten with sticks, hands, and feet. One of the Serbs who was beating Softic told him, "Death to the Muslims" was written there. Close to the witness another man was lying dead with his hand cut off, which the Serbs were kicking around on the ground. The Serbs tried to make Softic get up and run but Softic was too weak due to the meeting which he had received. On one occasion Softic tried to get up and accidentally kicked something which rolled within a few feet of the witness. It was a man's head.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Softic eventually managed to get up and run away, as ordered. After he had run about 30 metres, the witness saw a person named Hadjukovic shoot him in the back. Niski walked over to Softic and started to kick his head, presumably to see if he was really dead. Niski walked over to the witness and showed him the brain and blood on his foot and told the witness that soon his brain would be on the other foot. The Serbs then proceeded to beat the witness with cables, a plumbing tube, and a stick with a nail in it. The witness still bears the scars from this beating today. The witness declined to run when ordered, as he did not want to be shot. Eventually, the witness fainted from the beating. For the next four days and nights, different groups used to come into the building and beat all the detainees. The groups included Arkan's men, Seselj's men, the Yellow Wasps, Beli Orlovi, and others. Detainees were taken out of the room, ordered to run, and then machine-gun bursts could be heard. The witness presumed that they were shot like Softic. Each day at 1.00 p.m. the detainees were allowed, one by one, to go to the toilet which was located about 30 metres away. Most had to crawl because they had been so badly beaten. On one occasion the witness, whilst crawling to the toilet, saw the detainee who had left before him dead on the ground. The witness was in a bad state on account of the beatings and asked the guard escorting him to kill him. The guard, however, told the witness that he could not do as the witness had asked because the witness had been sentenced to death by torture and not by bullet. During the four days which the witness spent at Ekonomija, seven men were killed on the terrace on the way to the toilet. The witness was glad when this happened, as he thought that he would be the next to be shot. On one occasion, four or five of Arkan's men, including Jasikovac, a Serb from Loznica, came with a long wooden spit which was sharpened at the top. Abdulah Buljubasic was ordered to kneel down with his head against the wall. Two of Arkan's men then pushed the spit about 40 centimetres up into the anus of Buljubasic who screamed horribly before fainting. The witness saw blood coming from Buljubasic's anus and later heard that he was buried by his father. On another occasion, four or five of Seselj's men came into the building and took out Bego Bukvic. The witness heard him being ordered to run and then heard shots. Bukvic, however, a few minutes later, was dragged back into the room with a cross cut on his back, a bullet wound in each leg, and a broken arm. He was then stabbed in his hand and shot in the neck in front of the witness. Once a dead body which had been blown up and shot by the Chetniks was brought into the room. The detainees were ordered by four or five of Arkan's men to get down on their hands and knees and lick the blood from the body. The witness refused and had cigarettes put out on him and his throat cut as a punishment. Another detainee who refused to lick the blood had his ear cut off and was made to eat it. He was about 20 years old. A local Chetnik who was kinder to the detainees told them that Arkan's men were leaving the next day so it would be better for them. He also told them how they were sentenced. Basically, "Judge" Ilic took a list of their names and then, without reading the list, decided that those on page 1 would be shot to death, those on page 2 slaughtered, and those on page 3 tortured to death. This part concerns the release of the witness. At 11:00 or 12.00 a.m., a JNA truck stopped in front of the building and ten soldiers dressed in camouflage led by a captain entered the building. The soldiers all had Serbian flag badges on their caps. The men were ordered onto the truck. The first three men were so weak that they had to be thrown on by the soldiers. The group were loaded on top of each other. The witness was the last to be thrown on. Those people on the bottom cried out in pain and tried to get out of the truck, but the soldiers prevented them from doing so by hitting them with rifle butts. The truck headed towards Zvornik. The men below him stopped crying and moving. This was because they were dead. The witness was thrown out at the JNA barracks, and the truck moved off in the direction of Divic. At the headquarters, Sekanic and Pavlovic saw the witness and sent him to the hospital for rehabilitation. Pavlovic met him at the hospital, and he was treated by two doctors who spoke Serbian. His X-rays were taken, and he was found to have four broken ribs, a broken arm, and severe injuries to the head. He was kept in hospital for about four days. On the third day, a Muslim nurse told him to run away as the Muslims in the hospital were going to be killed and that he was marked by his pyjamas. He noticed that all the Chetniks had blue pyjamas whilst his were striped. A little later, two groups of Serbs visited his ward. One group was Captain Dragan and some of his men whilst the others were Chetniks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The witness pulled up the sheets to his nose so that they could not see his pyjamas and was able to escape detection. A Muslim nurse told him he was lucky as an ambulance driver and three children had been killed that morning. The witness left Zvornik hospital on 19th of May, 1992, and returned to his village in Zvornik. On 15th of June, all the people in his village were forced to sign a document saying that they had given up their property to the Serb authorities by their own free will. One day later, they were deported by the Chetniks to Vienna via Subotica. At the end of May, beginning of June, the witness saw Serbs unloading bodies from trucks into a mass grave at Ramin Grob, which was close to his house. Now, that, in essence, is the witness's statement. I would not propose to offer any exhibits through this witness, but I would, with the Court's permission, like to ask him a couple of oral questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness B-1780, I'm now going to ask you a couple of questions which you can kindly answer for me. Now, in your statement, you mention that you were sentenced by a Judge Ilic. Can you tell the Court where Judge Ilic's court was located in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Did you ever appear before him and argue your case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: How, if at all, would the SDS leadership in Zvornik have been aware of the activities of Judge Ilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He was the president of the SDS in his local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So according to you, there would have been communication between him and the SDS leadership of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, finally, Witness, you mentioned in your statement Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: What position of authority was Marko Pavlovic holding in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic was commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That would conclude my evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I start my cross-examination, I should like to make an objection, because I believe that it is absolutely impermissible the way in which Mr. Khan uses the term "Serbs." He describes some tortures here that allegedly occurred. He may talk about a formation, a military, paramilitary unit, a group of bandits, but every time he uses the term "Serbs." I think it is your duty to caution him that that is absolutely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel's name is in fact Mr. Agha. If he had done anything wrong, he would have been cautioned. He's been told earlier about not asking leading questions. And if he used terms which were derogatory unnecessarily, again he would be cautioned. No doubt he will avoid doing so if it were true that he did so. But in any event, it makes no difference as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned. We're well able to ignore anything of that sort. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to mention that my wording is not actually meant to cause offence, it is actually the wording which is gleaned from the statement of the witness. So I'm actually trying to summarise what is written rather than add my own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1780 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that this is a protected witness, so I cannot ask him about his positions in open session. Rather, no questions that could reveal his identity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is right. If you want to ask him any such questions, we must go into private session to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1780, in your statement you mention various people, Branko Grujic, the president in Zvornik, Ljubko Ilic, Dragan Tanic, et cetera. Are they all people from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then at the very beginning -- or maybe it was Mr. Agha who read out in the summary, but anyway, at the very beginning it was said that three or four men were practising shooting in a quarry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are they from Zvornik too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they came to practice shooting in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They were working for Grujic. They were cutting wood in the bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were workers from Grujic's bakery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. But later on, I saw them with Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into who you saw them with, but how did you know whether they were linked to Arkan's men or not? I'm not asking you about that either, but it is quite obvious that you cannot call them Arkan's men if they were workers in a bakery in Zvornik cutting wood there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They came there a month previously. They didn't used to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you noticed them a month earlier, working there and cutting wood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you later called them Arkan's men, though you don't have any evidence to say that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They were all wearing uniforms, and they were acting in the same way as they, and they spoke the Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: People from Zvornik were working in Serbia and speaking Ekavian and this didn't mean anything. So the people cutting wood certainly were not fighters but simple workers. If somebody is cutting wood, he's an ordinary labourer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That was just Grujic's trick. He brought them there earlier on to get acquainted with Zvornik. They would walk around Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, we saw it. I saw them. Everyone saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will come to that later. You say that you knew this Ljubko Ilic, that you knew him well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that he threatened you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you even say that he said that he hated his mother because she was a Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. I heard him saying that. He was drunk when he said that, and he started crying because he was in a drunken condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this reaction of his part of a general climate that is typical for a civil war that was under way there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you in Muslim paramilitary units? Because according to my information, you were later charged of killing people in Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That was the indictment against me. I didn't even go to Kula Grad. I couldn't go there. I couldn't reach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is not at issue, that you were charged of killing people at Kula Grad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They asked me which Serb I had killed at Kula Grad. I said that I hadn't been there at all, and I hadn't. I didn't move anywhere from my own house. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were active in politics, so surely you wouldn't engage in political work in your own home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the owner of the Rojal cafe, Sead Hadziabdic, in Drinjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You hadn't heard of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of Saban Redzic and Esad Haskic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Saban Redzic? I heard of him, and not of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This one is owner of the Rojal coffee bar. You don't know of that coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with coffee bars at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this one that you heard of, do you know that he engaged in illegal arming of members of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He worked before the war in the municipality as a civil construction inspector. I know nothing else about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the name Samir Nisovic, who had a nickname, Captain Almir? Do you remember the name Samir Nisovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I only heard of Captain Almir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was he the organiser of the Patriotic League in this area based in Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember Midhat Grahic? Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: There are several Grahics in Zvornik. I heard of him but I don't know about this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He headed a unit called the Dzamijski Golubovi, or the Mosque Doves, and they were active as so-called fighters for the faith. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the period you're testifying about; in the autumn of 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about the Masked Doves, the fighters for the faith? You only heard about Grahic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I heard of the Mosque Doves during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about them during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I just heard about them. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you knew that they weren't doves but a military unit. Surely you have an idea what they represented.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They were some sort of a military unit, but I wasn't there, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about this military unit and their activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I wasn't in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar with another group known as the Kobras, under command of a certain Suljo who used to be a teacher in Sapna? Sulejman Terzic is his name. Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I heard of the Terzic surname, but I don't know about Sulejman Terzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that he was in command of this paramilitary group known as the Kobras?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this generalised climate of sabre rattling and the activities of these groups, did this fan fear and hatred? Is that why your neighbour threatened you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He didn't threaten just me. He threatened others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did he threaten you? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He said, "He will be mine." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did he say that to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He told my other neighbours that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. He didn't dare say such a thing to me. He did it secretly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he didn't threaten you, but he told your other neighbours in secret that he would kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He had a shop. He worked as a merchant. And when my neighbours dropped in in his shop, then he would start talking politics. And if I would happen to pass by, he would say, "That one there will be mine."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about Ljubko Ilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, Ljubko Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agha asked you about him. Where was he a judge? Do you know whether he was a judge at all, or maybe he wasn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I was told this by a Serb soldier in the camp, that Ljubko Ilic was the judge who had condemned me to death by torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He described that this alleged judge, this would-be judge, passed judgement in such a way that going along the list, the first page to be killed, the second page to be slaughtered, and the third page to be tortured. So simply according to the names listed on each page. He didn't examine anyone, he just decided like that. You described all that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, in answer to a question from Mr. Khan, you said that you were never taken before that judge and that you never saw that. You were never taken before the judge. Then how could you see him doing -- passing judgement by page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I was told this by a Serb solder in the camp, that I was on the list for torture. "That's how Ljubko Ilic, the judge, has sentenced you," he said. That is how I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You describe with precision how this would-be judge passed judgement by turning over pages, without looking at the names, saying this first page to be killed, the second tortured, et cetera. Yes. And did all this -- did this Serb soldier tell you all this about this judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He told me that I was on the list for torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where did you get this story from that this judge passed judgement in this way by page, first page in one way, second page another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago that this soldier told me that. This was a young man, he was a minor, who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not only did he tell you that you were on the list for torture but he also explained the technology of work by this would-be judge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. And this soldier brought us bread in the prison, this Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was the soldier there a guard at your prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And his duty was to bring you food, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, the others didn't, but he brought it in from his own home and would just throw it in to us, just a bit, and he told us not to tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anybody about what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he would bring in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like a suitable moment to adjourn. We're going to adjourn now, Witness B-1780, for 20 minutes. During the adjournment, would you please remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. We'll sit again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The soldier you mentioned, saying he brought you bread, did he bring you the bread every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. Perhaps a couple of times. He didn't bring it in to me but to all of us who were there, and that might have been half a kilo of bread, and he would throw it in to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how many times did he bring you the bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Maybe a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So does that mean twice, three times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know. Two or three times. But it was stale bread, bread several days old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say he threw the bread in to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when did you have time to talk to him and for him to tell you about these judgements and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, he stood at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he only talk to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He talked to us because there was nobody else to talk to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he there all the time with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many days was he with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he'd be there for a few hours and leave and come back to take up his shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many days did you see him there actually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I didn't count the days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his name was, the soldier's name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. All I know is that he was underage, or at least he looked like a minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that the conflict in Zvornik began on the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the day when the Republican Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina passed a decree with respect to the Territorial Defence headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the mobilisation of the Muslim police took place, which the SDA, Abdulah -- member Abdulah Pasic and Nenad Sabic [phoen], commander of the TO staff, made the decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know. There was no mobilisation. I didn't hear about it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of organisation on the Muslim side at the time on the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, there wasn't, because they didn't believe there would be any kind of aggression at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did the Serbs, if there was no mobilisation in the village of Celopek, several kilometres downstream from Zvornik, set up a unit of their own if there was nothing happening in Zvornik, no activities on the part of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know about Celopek. I wasn't there, so I don't know. And it was a long way from where I was, and I'm hearing what you say for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a response to what was going on to Zvornik on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, nothing was happening in Zvornik on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you talk about what you experienced and lived through at the hands of your neighbours. Was that a sort of revenge for what had happened before that? For example, do you know about the killing of the soldier in Sapna on the 5th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I heard about that over the radio. Now, whether it was retaliation, I don't know. I don't think it was revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that your neighbours took you off to Karakaj, to an old factory farm called Stara Ekonomija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they asked you to write down how many Serbs you had killed at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask anybody else to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know. They just -- I just know that they asked me and my neighbour Softic to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they asked you and your neighbour to do that. Right. Now, do you happen to remember what date that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: The 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know about the attack on the 17th of April, 1992, when the armed forces of the SDA party launched an attack on the Serbian village of Rastocnica in the Zvornik municipality, when Zoran Bogdanovic, a Serb, was killed, born in 1971. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. It's a long way away from me. It's 20 kilometres away from me and I know nothing about that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about the attack on the Serbian village of Boskovici on the 5th of May, 1992 when nine civilians were killed? And I have their names here. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm hearing of that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the 9th of May, 1992, of an attack on the village of Gornja Boljkovica when 16 Serbs were killed? All this took place after the Muslim mobilisation organised by the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. That's the first time I hear of it. All this is new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that particular occasion these SDA forces completely destroyed and burnt down the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I've never heard of anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't heard of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have here, for example, a document from the committee gathering data of the crimes committed against humanitarian law, and it was compiled on May 2001 for the Zvornik municipality, and it lists 127 casualties, victims who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think the witness has seen a copy of this document, or even perhaps it's been exhibited before the Court, and I'm not quite sure how he could comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He'll be asked about it. If he can't comment, he'll say so. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we have here the victims of the first -- of the period you're talking about, the last days of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, and there are 127 names on this list, and there are some markings next to their names, next to their numbers, for comparison purposes, comparison with other lists. They have no significance. But take a look at this list, please, and tell me if you recognise any of the victims listed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to hand the witness this list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And starting with the events I've already listed, there were a large number of people killed. This particular list has 127 names on it, and they were killed precisely during the period of time that you're testifying about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Under number 99, Simo Savic from Gornja Boljkovica, the Zvornik municipality. That man didn't live in Boljkovica, he lived in Zvornik, and I know him as a pensioner. He was retired before the war. Now, where he was killed, I really don't know. So I recognise that name, but I don't know any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you only know that one man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Savic, under number 99.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, Mr. May, would you be so kind as to include this list amongst the exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness knows nothing of the list, and it would seem to me more appropriate that this is produced by someone who can speak as to what it is and speak to its authenticity. This witness has no connection with it and knows nothing about it. Let the document go back. You can call evidence about it during your case, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he did recognise one name on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. He's in no position to comment further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, on the 12th of May, your neighbours took you off, and you say that they beat you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: On the 12th May, Ilic Ljubko took me away, and the other man was Petko Hajdukovic. The third man was nicknamed Niski. He wasn't my neighbour, he was a man from Serbia. There was a man called Tanic, also from Zvornik. So they were the men who took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the three of them were from Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they beat you and tortured you, and you mentioned some very monstrous things that were happening, as you claim. Don't you think that had that actually happened, the whole country would have known about it and news would have buzzed around about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just deal with this. Now, that is by way of a comment, but we need to understand this. Are you suggesting to this witness that those things that he alleged happened at the farm building to these detainees did not occur? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, these are such unbelievable things that I do absolutely doubt that anything like that could have been going on without anybody knowing about it. That's quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Wait a moment. The witness should certainly have the opportunity to deal with that. Witness B-1780, you hear what the accused suggests. He suggests that these outrages which you have described to the detainees at that farm did not take place at all. Now, this is your opportunity to answer and comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it all and experienced the same thing, and I have proof. I have scars on my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1780. Now, what you described happened at this factory farm, the Ekonomija, in a location which was not unknown; isn't that right? It was a well-known locality in the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume to all the locals. It was a factory farm, the Ekonomija, in the vicinity, and people must have known what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: It was situated in between two Serbian villages that factory farm, and nobody could approach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you claim, this was done by your locals and some people in various groups whom you didn't recognise, and you don't know where they're from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I know they spoke the Ekavian language. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that on one of these days, you will tell me when, that a group of JNA soldiers arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. Ten of them came with a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what day was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This was on the fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you said a moment ago that they had a Serb flag on their caps --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Instead of the five-cornered star, they had a small tricoloured flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that JNA soldiers couldn't wear a Serbian flag. They could only have worn a Yugoslav flag and not a Serb flag. Either they were not JNA soldiers or they were not wearing a Serb flag, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Instead of the five-cornered star they had a tricoloured flag on their cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said clearly that you saw them wearing a Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I said a tricolour flag instead of the five-cornered star.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't argue with you as to what it is you said. However, let us just compare some things from your statement. You say you were taken away on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 81, you say: "On the 15th of May I was taken to the Zvornik hospital."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: On the fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can count it from the 12th to the 15th of May, that's three days. So you couldn't have spent four days there, as you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: The 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th, that makes it four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all these events occurred in that short span of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you remember that one of them introduced himself as an Arkan man, that his name was Rambo, though we all knew that Rambo had been killed during the attack on the Kula Grad. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was a false introduction, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I heard on the Serbian radio Zvornik that someone called Rambo had been killed at Kula Grad, and then later on a man introduced himself as being Rambo. Now, I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just reading from what you say in paragraph 39. "One of Arkan's men called himself Rambo, although we all know that the real Rambo was killed during the attacks on Kula Grad."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's right. That is what was said on the radio, the Serbian radio Zvornik. Later on, this man said that he was Rambo. I don't know how many Rambos there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You couldn't find out who all these men were. Now, I'm looking at paragraph 38. You say,"Various groups came, they beat us." And then you list "Arkan's men, Seselj's men, White Eagles, Yellow Wasps, and Pejic's men. I did not know the difference, but some of the groups had long hair and beards. Some others didn't."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear that this was not the army of Republika Srpska or the JNA. Is that clear at least, Mr. 1780?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: The men who beat us, when they beat us, they would say, "You see how Seselj's men beat?" Then the next group when they beat, they would ask us, "Do you know who the White Eagles are?" And that is how I knew who they were. They themselves revealed who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, since you talk about a certain Sekanic, who is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: A lieutenant in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
