utterances.text: He came to Zvornik then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you said that you had handed your rifle to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This was sometime in April. He came with soldiers to our village, and those of us who had weapons surrendered them. There were hunters amongst us, and we handed in our rifles, and we had documents for those rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain to me now what you say in your statement in describing that a couple of days later a truck, a military truck, appeared, and you say that members of the army took you to the barracks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: What truck? What barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading paragraph 61 of your statement. "About 11:00 or 12.00, a JNA truck stopped in front of the building. Ten soldiers entered the room headed by captain --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness a copy of his statement? If not, he should have one. And if you would look at paragraph 61, you will see what it is the accused is referring to. If you would find 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says in paragraph 61, without repeating what I've already said, "A JNA truck stopped and soldiers entered headed by a captain who was carrying an automatic rifle. All of them were wearing camouflage uniforms. All of them had on their caps badges with the Serbian flag." And you wrote down what you said orally a moment ago, which means it's out of the question that they could have been JNA if they had the Serbian flag on their caps. Then towards the end of the paragraph, you mention a Colonel Sekanic; now you say he's a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, a lieutenant. This is a mistake. He was a lieutenant, Sekanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then this is a mistake. And then you add, since you say that this lieutenant was a JNA member: "Aleksandar Sekanic, known as Aco, was born in Bijeljina."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he is from your area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "This was in 1992 when I gave Aleksandar a hunting rifle. He was together with Captain Cale from Sabac." So this man whose name was Sekanic was from your area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, he wasn't from my area. He was from Bijeljina. He said himself he was from Bijeljina, but I was an officer of the JNA. That's what he said. So he was from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, many were in the JNA before the war, even those who were later of the -- belonged to the army of Republika Srpska, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the HVO. I assume you know that, Mr. 1780.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He told me that he was a JNA soldier from before, that he -- before the war, that he used to be a soldier of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you say that a couple of days later, that is, rather, when they took you away from the Ekonomija that they subjected you to a normal interrogation by people who inquired about some killings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Which people? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 69 -- 68. You say: "He called me an Ustasha and told me to put my hands on the table. He pointed his rifle at me and asked me how many Serbs I had killed." And then in paragraph 69, you say: "I told him that I had never killed anyone. At that moment, Sekanic entered the office and asked me what I was doing there, who had brought me, and why I was so beaten up. I didn't dare tell him anything. So I just said I didn't know." Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I didn't dare say that anyone had beaten me. I had to say that I had fallen and hurt myself, because I know if somebody said that he had been beaten, he would be killed straight away, and that is why I didn't dare say that anyone had beaten me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So none of the horrors that you described as having taken place at the Ekonomija previously, you didn't tell them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "At that moment another JNA officer entered the room, gave me his hand and said he was Major Marko Pavlovic, the commander."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's right. He said, "I'm the commander here."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he wasn't a JNA officer either but a commander of the Zvornik Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He came from Serbia. From Zrenjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into where he had come from, but he was not a member of the JNA. Is that clear or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He said that he was the commander there. And I know that he had come from Serbia, from Zrenjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 71, you say: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they took you to hospital. Major Pavlovic stood in front of the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say they put you to bed, they gave you injections and pills, and you spent four days in the prison hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that in the prison hospital, they wanted to kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain, please, they take you to hospital, they treat you there, they know who you are. Why would they treat you, take X-rays to see whether you have any injuries, keep you in hospital, and then try and kill you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They intended to send me back to the camp down there, and this was a trick of theirs. They would pretend to be helping you and then they would kill you. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these horrific events that you describe, it's quite illogical that if they had wanted to kill you, they would have killed you over there. On the contrary, they took you to the hospital and treated you there and then released you home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They intended to send me back there. I was saying this was a trick of theirs. They would pretend to be helping you, and then they would send you there to be killed. And it was thanks to the intervention of my wife that I was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how, then, did you manage to survive if they really had intended to kill you and they treated you in hospital, and now you say this treatment in hospital was a trick.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't treat me at all. I didn't feel any better. They gave me some injections, but I wasn't better at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They gave you pills and injections.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, they gave me some yellow pills, but they didn't improve my condition at all. This was a trick. They would pretend to be treating you for others to see, and then they would send you away to be killed. Not just me, but everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that. Will you please explain. Who did they kill in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: A nurse, a Muslim. They wouldn't let her go home. She worked there before the war and she had to stay there, working. She whispered to me that a group was going through the hospital killing all Muslims, and she said that that was the order. And she told me, "Go to your room, put a blanket over you so they wouldn't see your pyjamas, which were marked," and that is what I did. And that is how I survived. They came by later on, they didn't recognise me. And I know that they killed a driver on that occasion who was a driver in the hospital. He was wounded. He had three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you spent four days in hospital, and for four days they didn't try to kill you, and on the 19th of May they released you to go home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't really release me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you escape from hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. This nurse told me that I had to escape. And as soon as they left, I told the doctors, when they came visiting, I said I was feeling better and that I could go. And they told me to get up. I got up and left. I went outside. I was in the corridor, and they put another man in my bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they released you to go home or did you run away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: The doctor told me to get up. I got up and walked to the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you went home in pyjamas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. I saw another woman there who was working as a cleaning lady. She was a Muslim too. And she found some clothes for me. She changed me, because I couldn't do it myself, and that is how I walked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's normal for a nurse to help you to dress as you were hurt; but you didn't run away from the hospital, you were released, because you said you felt better.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I said I felt better in order to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't they have plenty of chances to kill you if they really had wanted to kill you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I'm telling you this was a trick. They would pretend to help you, and then they would send someone else to kill you. That is how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have a single example of somebody being treated by such a trick and then someone sent to kill him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't send people to kill me but all the Muslims in hospital, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they kill those Muslims in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I know they killed three children and a driver who used to drive in the hospital, and he was wounded too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 80, you say that: "Later on, the same nurse, Najfa Delibajic, told me that I was lucky to be alive because they had killed three children and a driver of an ambulance."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, he was a driver in the hospital, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Ramo, the X-ray technician who worked in the Zvornik hospital, told me about those killings."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He told me that. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the ambulance driver wasn't in the hospital at all when he fell casualty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He was lying in the hospital wounded. Now, where he was actually wounded, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you went home and nobody stopped you going; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I took the safe road home, another road, not the one I usually take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then after the 16th of June, you found yourself in Subotica in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of June, I arrived in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you found your salvation in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't want to go to Serbia and go to Vienna via Serbia, is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: On the 15th of June, 1992, we signed a piece of paper saying that we voluntarily gave all our property to the Serb authorities, and they rounded us up in two buses on the 15th of June. They came to my village and deported us via Mali Zvornik, Sabac, to Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were in a refugee camp in Subotica, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you given Yugoslav passports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I wasn't. I had a passport from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So did you yourself decide to go to Vienna or were you deported there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They put us onto a train and let us leave. They didn't tell us where we were going. We didn't know where we would go, but we ended up in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as a refugee, you found yourself in Serbia. You were a free man there, free to walk around wherever you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I wasn't there of my own free will. They deported us as far as Subotica and for us to go on further from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, did anybody restrict your freedom in Serbia in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: We weren't allowed to leave the camp anywhere, the Subotica camp. It was at Palic, on Mount Palic, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you went to Vienna if you weren't allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: An army escort and a police escort. There were some policemen there and some soldiers there, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they escorted you to Vienna, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, just to the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means they transported you from the refugee camp to the train, and you were free to go where you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, the train's destination was Hungary and then further on to Vienna. Nobody asked us whether we wanted to get on, we just got onto the train and went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But did anybody in any way whatsoever do any harm or injustice to you in Serbia while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, there were just threats. A man called Djuro. Djuro was a guard in the camp. All I know is that they called him Djuro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the refugee camp? There were no guards who would control refugees. You were taken care of there in the camp which was under the supervision of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: It wasn't the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it then? Was it a concentration camp, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it was, but we got there and weren't allowed to leave. And this man Djuro said, "I can kill anybody who leaves." And I don't know any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1780, nobody in Serbia anywhere was ever killed, none of the refugees from any of the staff members in a refugee camp or anything like that, any refugee collection centre or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, we weren't refugees who wanted to go there. We were brought in there for us to be sent further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you left further of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't go to Vienna because you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. We were ordered to board the train and go further. Nobody told us where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you crossed the border and found yourselves in Hungary. Could you go to Vienna or any other place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: When we boarded the train it was already dark, night-time, and we spent the whole night on the train. We reached Budapest, and we didn't want to get out there in Budapest. So we continued our journey to Austria, because we heard that it would be better for refugees to go to Austria rather than stay in Hungary. Those were the rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as you left hospital on the 19th of May, 1992, where did you go after that, and how come you testified about watching some burials take place? Were you at your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, that was several kilometres from Zvornik, according to this information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My house is several kilometres away from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how were you able to watch these Serbs burying the Muslims? How were you able to assess that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: It was our cemetery, the local cemetery in our area, and you can see it clearly from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you make a diagram indicating the positions of some mass graves at the mass cemetery? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because some of my family members are buried there and so are my neighbours, and I know the cemetery by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you watch the burials take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it all personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, as you commented on the map of the -- and the ethnic composition of Zvornik, drawn up by Himzo Tulic, what has that map got to do with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: What's it got to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, it's a piece of information to show how many of the different groups there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says the municipality, 81.111 and 30.000-odd Muslims, 48.000 Croats, 120 Yugoslavs, 1.022 of the others.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what's that got to do with the events you're describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: As I say, it's just a piece of information, facts and figures, to show how many inhabitants belong to what ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you told me about your passport, in point 82 you say the following: "They boarded us up into a bus and took us to Subotica where we spent two days in the refugee camp." So you there for a total of two days. And then you go on to say, "We were given Yugoslav passports." And then you go on to say, "We arrived in Vienna on the 19th of June by train."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, if anybody didn't have a passport, they must have had a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you used the first person plural and say, "We were given refugee --" "We were given passports." So as refugees, you were given passports, and all this procedure lasted for two days and then you went where you wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: So what? What's strange there? You couldn't pass the border crossing without a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that I assume you're not challenging that they helped you in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That wasn't help. We paid for those passports. If you didn't have a passport you paid for it, and we were made to go there. We didn't go there because we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying how you reached Serbia, but once you were in Serbia, they treated you completely normally; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: It wasn't normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you were given accommodation and fed and given passports that enabled you to go wherever you wanted to go, that wasn't normal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, it wasn't normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What should they have done, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, they threatened us there, that we weren't allowed to go out, to move around, and they could kill us if we did, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to ask you any more questions about that. There's no point in doing that. In point 34, you refer to the following: A man wearing a light brown uniform with police insignia on the arm, and you say: "I know that that was not the normal type of Yugoslav police uniform that was worn"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this man wearing police insignia did not belong to the Yugoslav police force.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He was wearing police insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't a police uniform, was it? So that man couldn't have been a policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: He just had a police insignia on him. Now, whether he was a policeman or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say it wasn't the customary type of uniform worn by the Yugoslav police force.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me just this now, please: You say in point 36 that you don't know how many of them "jumped on me." "There might have been ten to 15 of them or maybe more." Now, how is that possible? How can anybody survive ten to 15 people jumping on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't only jump all over me but all over the others too, and there were ten to 15 of them. Perhaps not every -- each single one of them jumped all over me, but they could hit me, they kicked me. And I have injuries and scars that are still visible on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that you were hurt, but a moment ago when you were asked about the officer that interrogated you and then took you off to hospital, you said you didn't want to tell them what had happened to you because you were afraid and that the explanation you gave was that you fell and hit and hurt yourself. So those injuries on you must have been terrible had 15 people jumped all over you, and yet you said that some -- that you hit yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: We didn't dare say that anybody had beaten us. You had to say that you fell and hit yourself. That's what we were told. And if anybody said who hit him, he would be killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of somebody who said he was beaten and then was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Give us this example of somebody owning up to being beaten and then being killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: There's a man here, Bego Bukvic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he killed because he said that he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, when he told them who had beaten him, they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not what it says here. Read out what it says.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, I know that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't write that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: What I said was that he was taken out and killed, and I know the reason why he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it should be clear to anybody reading your statement if you don't actually write it down and say so in your statement. Mr. 1780, you spent four days in the camp, you say, and then four days in the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went to the camp on the 12th, and you were released from hospital on the 19th. So from the 12th to the 19th is not eight days. And you describe a series of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a point where you misunderstand the mathematics, I think. Anyway, it is a point of no significance at all. Let us try and move on. Now, you've had longer than the usual time for the reason that the Prosecution have not got sufficient witnesses so we're not under the usual pressure of time, but there must come a time when this cross-examination is brought to an end, and it's been fairly circular. So the conclusion is that we'll give you another ten minutes and then you must conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in point 38, towards the end, that members of certain groups would enter the premises -- "for them to enter the premises, we would have to sing Chetnik songs to welcome them." Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I did write that, and I sang the songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what kind of Chetnik songs did you have to sing and did you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does this really matter? He's explained in general terms what the position was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is important, Mr. May, because quite obviously it's not true. That's why it's important, because some things here can't be the truth, and then we come to the question -- the general question of what is the truth at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested that you sang -- your saying that you sang Chetnik songs is untrue. Perhaps you'd like to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true. I did sing them. And I had to make the sign of the cross and to make the sign of the three fingers raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So which Chetnik songs did you sing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: We sang Vojvoda Sindjelic, both songs. And, "Those who say that Serbia is small are telling lies to us all." And we had to learn the Lord's Prayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had to do all that while they were torturing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for this song Vojvoda Sindjelic, that is a popular song which dates back to the -- it is a folksong about Vojvoda Sindjelic who fought against the Turks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs sang that song, and we had to sing it too. And you could hear the song being sung in Zvornik over the Serb radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So why are you calling that song a Chetnik song?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Because the Chetniks sang it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people singing it were Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You call them Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at my notes. Tell me, please, in point 45, you say that four or five Arkan's men arrived. How do you know they were Arkan's men, and did Arkan's men go to those parts at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I do know because they had different uniforms and different caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You enumerated Arkan's men, the White Eagles, the Yellow Wasps, Pejic's men, Seselj's men, and so on. And then you -- actually, you enumerate all these units. So tell me, how many men came to that factory farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, anybody that could came by. So all those units came by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But how many people did you see there in all these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I didn't count, but they would come in groups of five, six, four, ten, depending, 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the ten to 15 that jumped all over you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't jump only over me, they jumped all over everybody else too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please: You say that Captain Dragan came to visit you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't visit me. He came into the room I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he came to visit the wounded in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know why he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what other reason could there have been apart from his visiting the wounded in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: You would have to ask him that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you do know that Captain Dragan came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: When he left, one of the wounded asked the other, "Do you know who that was?" And he said, "Yes, I do. That was Captain Dragan," and swore at him, cursed his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he cursed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Well, it wasn't actually a swear word, it was just a way of talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, this is what he said. He said, "That's Captain Dragan, fuck him."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did Captain Dragan actually say? What was he doing in hospital except for visiting the wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, he asked them how they felt, how they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he came to visit the wounded to ask them how they were and then left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know whether he came to tour them. All he did was to come in and ask. Now, what his intentions in the hospital were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did he insult anybody or do anything that wasn't in keeping with a hospital visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, who could he insult?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were there, for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did he to talk to anybody especially?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he just went round visiting you and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: And he talked to some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did anything happen, any event happen or anything else that you could say -- that you had some criticisms to make of? Did anything untoward happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. I don't have any criticisms to make, and he didn't come up to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't come to anybody special, he went to the hospital to visit the wounded who were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know why he came. He just came into the room and asked individuals how they were, how they felt. Now, what his intentions were, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then what other intention could he have had except to visit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what he did after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1780. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would submit that the witness before you is precisely one of the cases when, in accordance with your ruling of the 6th of October, I could be of considerable assistance in clearing up a few matters before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you, Witness, if you could, to look at paragraph 65 of your statement that you have in front of you. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence in that paragraph, you speak of the truck which, together with the nine men that you mentioned when examined by the Prosecutor, you said that the men who were at the bottom stopped crying, but they also stopped moving. They had died. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 10th of July of this year, together with the statement that is before the witness, I also received a statement which the witness gave to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina shortly after these events on the 27th of December, 1992. I have a photocopy of that. I also have an English translation in three copies as the statement has been translated into English. So could this statement be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let it be shown to the witness, and we'll look at the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this your statement, is this your signature at the end of this statement, a statement given on the 27th of December, 1992, to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: It is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know that until I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness just look at the statement, and perhaps we could have the copies which you said were in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three copies in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You signed that statement at the bottom of each page. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I need to read it out entirely to know whether it is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just have a quick look at it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps you could just have a quick look at it, Witness B-1780, for these purposes. Do you remember making the statement? Witness B-1780, do you remember making the statement or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did make this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, counsel may be going to ask you about one or two passages. Just see what he asks, and of course you can have a chance to read then before you answer, but he'll refer you to the passages he has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the English version, it is the third paragraph, and in the Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian it is the second paragraph of the statement you have in front of you. It is paragraph 2 on page 3. In the English version, third paragraph from the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last page. From the end of the English statement. So the third paragraph from the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't dwell on this too much, Mr. Witness. You're referring to the 16th of May as the day you went to the hospital. It's a mistake. I won't insist on that. But I would like to draw your attention to the following: You were speaking about some special units there. You didn't mention the JNA. Could you tell us who those special units were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: That is the group of soldiers that came with the captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention the Yugoslav People's Army here. You called them the specials. But that's not the reason why I'm asking you this. Look at the following sentence: When you entered the truck, "the prisoners were ordered to lie on the floor of the truck. The first three, then the next three on top of them, and the last three on top of them." Is that right? "I was the tenth, and I was ordered to sit on top of all of them." Is that right? "They said they would get the other eight, that they would come from the other eight." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They said that they would come for the others. Maybe the eight is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them or to the nine. You said that you didn't know what happened to those nine, because you say here that, "When we arrived in Zvornik, I was taken off the truck and the truck went on its journey." So in this statement you said that you didn't know what happened to those nine men, and today you were saying that those beneath you all died. Now, what is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Both is true. When I say I didn't know where they went, I didn't know where they took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, next paragraph. How far is your house from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Couple of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How much time did it take for you to get home from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Normally I would can get there in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said here explicitly that you had escaped from the hospital, which is different from what you said here today, but even that doesn't matter. What I think you should explain to Their Honours from this statement - two more points - because in two paragraphs above this in the English version and in the last paragraph of the version in front of you, you said -- in the middle it says: "They cut a cross on my cheek." Today and in an earlier statement, you said that the cross was cut for someone else, not on your cheek. Was it on your cheek? Did you -- did they see that at hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: No. This was more like a scratch. It wasn't very deep on my cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that a cross, the sign of the cross was cut into your cheek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And the same was done to Bego Bukvic, on his back, and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then further on - I won't dwell too much on that - but in paragraph 55 of the statement you gave here, you say: "At the same time while we were being punished, the others had to lick the blood from the body of this young man," that they wanted you to do the same but you refused. However, in the statement you gave in 1992, after this business with the cross, you say: "Then they would lick our blood." You didn't say that anyone forced you to do that. How can you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This man Niski, the man they called Niski who had the rank of major, he made this cross with a knife on me, and then he licked the blood off his knife, looking me in the eye. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So let us now go back to the things that you testified about today. For instance, paragraph 27. You spoke of the hand that was cut off, and you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 29, you speak of a head that was kicked around.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 32, of the execution of a certain number of men. Then in paragraph 44, the seven killed men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: There was a total of seven killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 52, you said that there were cases when the skin between the fingers was cut with a knife. That was the punishment for those who refused to lick blood. Then you speak of an ear, and then in paragraph 54, you say that a man was scalped. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Scalped?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the term you used. Paragraph 54 I think it is. But never mind. Tell me, now if could you explain to Their Honours, do you have the name of any one of these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Which men?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The victims, except for the killing of Bego and Ramiz Softic. Do you have the name of any of the perpetrators or any one of the victims who lost their lives in that way? And is there any witness who saw these things apart from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Abdulah Buljubasic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask you about that. He was the man who, according to you, suffered a terrible death.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you have his first and last name; Abdulah Buljubasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: And his father buried him, Bego Buljubasic. He's alive in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The father of that man buried his own child.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And his grave is known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I don't know it, but the father knows. The father does know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You gave this statement in 1996, and it could easily be established what was the cause of death of that particular person. So the Court could rule and decide without any doubt whatsoever. So even that was not checked out by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution could have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, everyone must be responsible for his acts, and I'm sure that anyone who did such horrors must be punished adequately, and I'm sure you will do that. But it is my profound conviction that this Tribunal's prime role, or one of the most important roles, is for all of us over there in those areas to reconcile. And if such stories are presented here without a single piece of evidence or proof, then one must ask what the point of all this is. If there is proof - for instance, if he knew where these people were buried, if he knew about this mass gave - why wasn't that checked out? Why weren't the bodies exhumed? Even that was not done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not the time now for submissions. Yes. Now, you've made your point. Anything else, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Witness: Aren't these stories that were circulating in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you're putting into your statement as if you personally had seen it all and experienced it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: I saw and experienced all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If I may very briefly just ask a few points in clarification to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness B-1780, when was the first very first time that you were accused of killings in Kula Grad? And where was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: The first time when I was taken to the camp. That is what I heard it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And in which language was the written accusation made against you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: These were not written accusations. They told me to write down the number of Serbs I had killed at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now just move to a different area, which is Mr. Ilic who has been under much discussion in your evidence. Now, if you could just kindly turn to paragraph 5 of your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement. I believe that it's written there that: "At that time, he was -" and that's Mr. Ilic - "the president of the Serb court-martial in the Serb community of Zvornik municipality." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: A minor soldier told me that in the camp, a young soldier who was under age.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic? Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, and Mr. Agha too, used the term "court-martial," which means a military Tribunal, and it's been translated as "court-martial." I have no objection regarding Mr. Agha's explanation, because he used the term to be found in the transcript, but the proper translation of "court-martial" would be summary court, "preki sud," summary court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will have that checked out. It can be done in due course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The other area that I'd like to touch upon is that the accused finds it incredible that the events which you describe in your statement could have occurred, because everyone would have known about them. Now, I'm hoping not to lead here. Would Marko Pavlovic have known; and if so, how would he have known about Ekonomija farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Are you asking me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: As he introduced himself as the commander, he should have known. He must have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: But you mentioned that your wife had saved you. What was your meaning by that? Had she done anything in particular to ensure that your welfare was looked after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: This is how it was: When Lieutenant Sekanic came to collect the weapons in the village, he said, "You are safe now, and don't worry at all." Later on, my wife said to him, "You said that we would be safe, and what kind of an officer are you when you're lying, when you took them all away?" And that was reason why he took me out of the camp and to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness B-1780, the accused has disputed the time you spent in the camp, but you did go to the hospital. Now, how often did the hospital come and treat people at Ekonomija farm, if at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: They didn't come to treat. If somebody was bleeding profusely, they would take him to hospital, and later on they would bring him back with bandages.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Where was this hospital located which they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: In Zvornik. That is where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Who would have been in charge of paying the salaries and administering the hospital? Which authority would have been responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: Well, since the SDS party was in power, everything went through them. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one final question. When you were released from the camp and the hospital and you went home, how many times did you approach the authorities, the SDS authorities, to allow you to leave and go to Vienna or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1780
utterances.text: We didn't ask. I didn't ask them to let me go. I had to sign that I would make a gift of everything to the Serb authorities, and they organised the transportation for us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no more questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit the statement produced by Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll get the next C number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: C15, Your Honour. If the registry could have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the statement has been just admitted by one of the amici, may I also request that that should be put in under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, C15 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1780, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go, but just wait a moment while the blinds are put down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know if now or later would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's just about the rest of the day. The next witness is a witness who may not take very long, I understand. I believe you've been informed of our difficulties with the fourth witness, we'd hoped, for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then your legal officers were alive to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We were told in very general terms, Mr. Nice, but I would prefer that matters are dealt with openly, you know. It really is much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm not seeking to deal with it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position is that the fourth witness we had hoped to have available for today, who has been extremely cooperative on previous occasions when set up as a filler, B-1524, simply can't come today. There's been a change in personal circumstances and can't come at short notice. Tomorrow's witness, I already explained, was the witness for whom there were the passport difficulties, not of our creation at all, and I think that your legal officers have heard of that as well from Victims and Witnesses Unit. So we find ourselves in the position of not only having no witnesses tomorrow, apart from Mr. Blewitt, but possibly not even filling up the rest of today. I'm in a position to start Mr. Blewitt at any time, today or tomorrow. He can free himself from his other commitments, but I'm anxious, of course, not to, as it were, break into a day and have that day counted as fully used when this would not be for reasons that are within our control. As to administrative matters that might merit attention in court, there's a filing, I hope that will come your way by 2.00, in relation to the matter that's pending and perhaps fairly urgent. The application for additional witnesses will, I hope, be available this afternoon. There is some further work being done on that. Ms. Wee is dealing with that. I'm not aware of any other matters that necessarily require court time to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us first of all hear the next witness, then we will hear Mr. Blewitt, and then we'll deal with administrative matters. It would be a pity not to use what time is available for those matters which we can. One matter on which I would wish to be addressed tomorrow would be the question of finalising the exhibit list. We have in mind issuing an order to that effect, but we can discuss it generally tomorrow, and we will discuss, of course, matters of the witnesses. We will then determine how much of the day should count or not count against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be taking the next witness, B-1448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, by way of explanation, I think the wrong witness was brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be handed the 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's first of all get the blinds up and then we'll deal with the other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the first page of his statement in B/C/S, which is at the third page of tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, just look there at that page in front of you. Does that page accurately set out your name and personal details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, have you signed two statements taken by investigators from the OTP dated the 30th of March and the 18th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And did you further sign a declaration dated the 18th of November, 2001, by which you declared the contents of your written statements to be true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for the 92 bis package and associated exhibits to be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 579 with tab 1 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll read a very short summary. Witness B-1448 gives evidence that he was involved in one of the groups in the local communities in Brcko that formed to protect their homes and families. The group was attacked by Serbian forces on 16th, 17th of May, 1992, and during fighting, a Serb soldier was shot and killed. The witness was involved in the recovery of the dead Serb soldier's body. He found an ID card with the name Filipovic Branko on it, and in a military-type bag found on the dead body, several documents bearing the name Filipovic. He handed them in to an intelligence officer at the brigade HQ. The witness believes that six documents subsequently shown to him by the OTP are copies of those documents found by him. Your Honour, I have a couple of questions, additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, the documents which you removed from the military-type bag found by you and others, did you look at those documents each in turn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, did any of those documents stand out in your mind, having looked at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you describe to us broadly which of the documents stood out in your mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: One of those documents was similar to a travel log used before the war in the firm that I worked for and where I was a driver. You -- I'm sure you all know that if you drive for a company, you have to sign some receipts. So that would be the second document, this receipt. And the third document was a piece of information. And after I had taken this to the security officers in the brigade command headquarters, I took a closer look at those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, is this a travel log headed Military Post Number 9840 Brcko, and with the driver's name Branislav Filipovic written on it, valid from the 8th of May until the 31st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, that is one of the documents. It says here a travel log or a travel work document, but we called it travel authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, look at the second page of that document. Does the second page show the journeys undertaken by the vehicle about which this travel log is concerned dated 13th of May, 1992, from Brcko to Belgrade, and 14th of May, 1990 - although that must mean 1992 - from Bijeljina to Belgrade, amongst other journeys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, is this one of the documents that you recall taking, recovering from the dead Serb soldier's body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And is this a receipt headed Military Property Received for Temporary Use, with handwriting Military Post 5055 Belgrade, with at the bottom of the page a stamp for the military post number 5055 Belgrade, and is it identified as being received personally by B. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Does the document identify ammunition, including M57-shaped charge shells and other shells and hand grenades that were received personally by B. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, is this an authorisation permitting Branislav Filipovic to bring munitions from Belgrade to the Brcko garrison for the needs of the garrisons in Brcko and Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And does it say that it applies to types of ammunition, including ammunition for anti-aircraft guns, and is it signed on behalf of the garrison command in Brcko, Lieutenant Colonel Predrag Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are the only questions I had to ask of the witness. Before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to have the order which you refer to as limiting the scope of cross-examination. We do not have it to hand at the moment. We need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, is there anything else you want to ask, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, no further questions. Simply, if I could raise for Your Honours' attention, at paragraph 2 of the proofing summary I've simply identified there the sort of material that I would invite the Chamber to hear in private session should it come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I have now in front of me the order of the 10th of October to which you've referred.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, at paragraph 1 of the order, I think that's the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now for you to cross-examine the witness. Cross-examination in this case is limited, and has been by order, to the evidence concerning the discovery of the documents on the body of the dead soldier. That will, of course, include questions about the documents themselves if you wish to ask them. Apart from that, no other cross-examination. So this is a case of limited cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is the first time I hear about limited cross-examination. By stating that it is limited, it is limited under 92 bis, and now this is a limitation of the limitation, limited of the limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's better than admitting the written statement without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is of course true, but I don't see why the witness needs to appear here unless I can cross-examine him. But anyway, very well. I assume you'll draw my attention to my not asking him questions in that area, because the only limitation I understood was the one hour that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, Mr. 1448, in the first paragraph, you say that you were a member, and [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that group was a part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, was it, or was it a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Brcko, the group was not armed. However, due to force of circumstance in the ensuing period or, rather, in the month of May, a certain arming took place, a certain form of arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that, "When the war began in Brcko, I joined a group as were being set up in different communities for the protection of our homes and families."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is what Ms. Pack said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes. May I be allowed to answer, to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that group was indeed formed, but at the beginning of the war, it worked to pull out the infirm population and the population of the local community south of Brcko, the town itself, the territory of the Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If this was just a group set up for defence purposes and for protecting, as you say, the elderly and infirm, how come you had a brigade headquarters, which you refer to in paragraph 7? This is too large a formation for it just to be a collection of citizens defending their own thresholds.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: The brigade was formed later on in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're testifying to May, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, but the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to weapons, you yourself say in paragraph 3 that you had a Motorola radio station as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't that a little unusual for a group of citizens defending their threshold and taking out the infirm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I don't consider that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going outside the limitations. I've not stopped you asking about the group because they were involved in the search, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the witness mentioned arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the middle of 1991, the SDA party and the HDZ party in Brcko were organising joint training and arming for their members and that this arming was being done via the Savski Most-Sava bridge, in that area there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely for those purposes that at the checkpoint at the Sava bridge that Brcko policemen were deployed there who were members of the SDA and HDZ, and that they manned those checkpoints and had received detailed instructions from the commander, the chief of the public security station of Brcko and other officials, to provide security and ensure safety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going beyond the area which I've allowed cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that in procuring weapons or, rather, in financing the procurement, that private entrepreneurs from Brcko were quoted, such as Uso Bakor, Ramiz Vilic, Fikret Husic nicknamed Sok, Nesad Omerhodzic nicknamed Bedor [phoen], Meho Murhatovic [phoen], Dasko Carucevic [phoen], Husein Carucevic [phoen], Sefket Lubinovic nicknamed Lubin, and so on and so forth, and also some directors of socially owned companies. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I was a family man myself, and I wasn't burdened by party politics, any party. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you were within the armed formations and you went to the brigade headquarters, as you say with respect to your testimony here, in the distribution of weapons and the training of men, were the main protagonists of Uzeir Hajdanovic, Badi Hajdanovic [phoen], Sijos Kineskovic [phoen], Ramiz Pljakic, Kemal Hindic, and so on and so forth? Do you know these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that they saw to armament, the distribution of weapons, training, and so on, matters of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: As to what you're quoting Mr. Milosevic, I don't know about that, because as I've already said, from the beginning I was at -- shall we call it the front line. Now, what other people did, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the distribution of weapons to other local communes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, it's beyond the limitation; secondly, he can't answer it. So we're wasting time. Now let's go back to the questions which you can ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the training of sabotage groups conducted by Damil Suljic nicknamed Makija, Feto Mensur [phoen], Suljevic Nermin nicknamed Guminito [phoen], Tursic Muhamed nicknamed Hare, and others? Do you know anything about that? Do those names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: I know the names, the men, but what you're saying, Mr. Milosevic is not correct. There was no training. At least, I never saw any training going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now do you know about the continuous provocations when the Serbs were leaving the Stari Rasadnik local commune, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is just wasting time. You know the limitations. Now, if you want to ask this witness about the finding of the documents, you can. If you do not, we will go on and deal with other business.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will ask questions referring to the documents, [redacted] [redacted] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know what the limitations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of May, 1992, there was an escalation towards the Serbs and the JNA when there was an armed attack on the barracks in Brcko and the settlement called Srpska Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Once again, incorrect information. What I do know is that on the 1st of May, by the JNA and the paramilitaries, the local commune of Dizdarusa was attacked and the Brodusa local commune as well, and that they were shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no armed attack on the Brcko barracks and Varos settlement, Srpska Varos settlement, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes, I say that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement you say that the war in Brcko broke out at the beginning of May 1992, when, as you said, bridges were blown up across the Sava River. So who blew the bridges up and why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, you're not paying any attention and I shall stop your cross-examination altogether. You heard what the limitations were, and it's a matter for you whether you wish to ask any questions with them or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If this has been unsuited so far, Mr. May, as far as limitations are concerned, then just this soldier that was killed, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So tell me, please, Mr. 1448, in the pockets of that dead soldier you found a personal ID card to the name of Branko Filipovic with a photograph that corresponded to the image of the person killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in his bag you found some other documents mentioning Filipovic's name and the nickname Sumar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to what you said, in the ID card, and I seem to be the only one that hasn't been given it, it says Branko Filipovic in all the documents, that was the name that was written down. But in the photocopies I was given, it says Branislav Filipovic. Does that mean that the documents given to us in photo copy are not authentic or are you familiar with this dead Serb soldier and decided to give him this shorter name of Branko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar -- on familiar terms with him, and Branko is what it said. Now, whether it was Branko or Branislav, I don't think that is important. The sense of it, the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that a name has any sense, it is how it is written and articulated. Now, all the documents, including the ID card and all the other things from the bag, did you give it to the intelligence men in the brigade or did you keep the ID card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep it. It disappeared somewhere. Somebody else kept it, and I handed over all the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have an explanation of how it was only the ID card, which was the only document with the picture, wasn't -- hasn't been disclosed here with all the other documents, hasn't been handed over with all the other documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you describe in detail what the killed soldier had on him and with him, and you say he had a rifle and a pistol without any ammunition worthy of mentioning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I didn't say not worthy of -- not worth mentioning. There were two or three rounds, full rounds, in the rifle and in the pistol too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement the man had a rifle and pistol and there was no ammunition worth mentioning. I'm asking you that because that's what you say in your statement. "To speak of" was the term. And now you say that's not so. "He had a rifle and pistol, but there was no ammunition on him to speak of." That's what you say in paragraph 5 of your statement, at the beginning. "He had a rifle and pistol, but there was no ammunition on him to speak of." It is the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: What I meant was he didn't have a large quantity of ammunition, because as you yourself know, Mr. Milosevic, that one -- how many bullets one clip has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So that's why I was asking you, and you said that you didn't say "to speak of," so I read the sentence out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you take the rifle and pistol for yourself or did you hand it over to the brigade headquarters or any other place of authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I can't remember who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what you did with those weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1448
utterances.text: I said I didn't, but I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
